title: New Insights into Keeping Our Brains Agile with Age

paragraphs.text: The degeneration of the brain is far from inevitable. Its design features are such that it should continue to function for a lifetime, says Zaven Khachaturian, director of the Alzheimer’s Association’s Ronald and Nancy Reagan Research Institute in the USA. ‘There’s no reason to expect it to deteriorate with age, even though we are living longer lives.’ In fact, brain research has changed the opinions of many doctors, according to Stanford University neuroscientist Robert Sapolsky. ‘Thirty-five years ago, we thought Alzheimer’s disease was a dramatic version of normal aging. Now we realize it’s a disease with a distinct pathology.’

Activity seems to be the secret to keeping our brains agile and fit. This finding results in large part from a decade of research sponsored by the MacArthur Foundation Network on Successful Aging. In one study, Marilyn Albert of Harvard Medical School examined 1,192 healthy and mentally fit individuals between the ages of 70 and 80. ‘We looked at them in great detail,’ Albert says, ‘measuring everything from their blood pressure and cholesterol levels to psychiatric symptoms and whether they smoked.’ The seniors were tested in 1988 and again in 1991. A number of things were found to be related to their mental fitness: levels of education, physical activity, lung function, and feelings of self-efficacy. Each of these elements alters the way our brain functions, says Albert, who hypothesizes that regular exercise may stimulate blood flow to the brain and nerve growth, both of which render the neurons stronger and better able to resist disease. Moderate aerobic exercise, including long brisk walks and climbing stairs, will accomplish this.

Animal studies have also yielded interesting results in the area of brain function. At the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology in Urbana, Illinois, psychologist William Greenough observed rats playing with a number of toys. The rats developed about 25 per cent more connections between their neurons than did rats that didn't get any mentally stimulating recreation. In addition, rats that exercised on a treadmill developed more capillaries in specific parts of their brains than did their sedentary counterparts. This increased the blood flow to their brains. Clearly the message is to do as many different things as possible, Greenough says.

Education also seems to enhance brain function. People who have challenged themselves with at least a tertiary education may actually stimulate the neurons in their brains. Moreover, native intelligence may be advantageous for our brains. It is possible that intelligent people begin life in possession of more neurons, and therefore have a greater reserve to fall back on if some begin to fail.

Early linguistic ability also seems to help our brains later in life. A recent study in the New England Journal of Medicine looked at 93 elderly nuns and examined the autobiographies they had written 60 years earlier. The nuns whose essays were complex and dense with ideas remained sharp into their eighties and nineties.

Finally, personality seems to play an important role in protecting our mental prowess. According to Albert, there’s evidence that elevated levels of stress hormones may harm brain cells and cause the hippocampus, a small organ that’s a crucial moderator of memory, to atrophy. However, a sense that we can effectively chart our own course in the world may delay the release of stress hormones and protect us as we age. ‘It’s not a matter of whether you experience stress or not,’ Albert concludes, ‘it’s your attitude toward it.’

Neuroscientists have been researching exactly what happens to brain cells when their power begins to fade. What they’ve uncovered may eventually lead to a wide range of chemical approaches to preserving cognitive function. According to Doctor James McGaugh, who’s been working on memory-enhancing drugs for 40 years, there’s extensive laboratory evidence that animal recall is improved with drugs and hormones. But McGaugh notes that we’re still a long way from safely and accurately fine-tuning the brain with chemicals. The first generation of memory-improving drugs may be a breakthrough, yet their effect may be modest.

It’s not just scientists who are catching anti-aging fever. Walk into any health food store, and you’ll find nutritional formulas that claim to sharpen mental ability. Sales of ginkgo, an extract from the leaves of the ginkgo tree, which has been shown in published studies to increase oxygen in the brain and reduce the symptoms of Alzheimer’s disease, are up by 22 per cent in the last six months alone, according to Paddy Spence, president of a San Francisco-based market research firm.

Linda Gilbert, president of Health Focus, a company that researches consumer health trends, strongly believes that many of the products found in health food stores do increase and preserve mental performance. While neuroscientists like Khachaturian believe the use of these supplements is equivalent to the superstition of tossing salt over your shoulder, the public is nevertheless greedy for nutrients that promise cognitive enhancement.

options.text: several criteria are linked to mental health.
walking is the best form of exercise for old people.

options.text: have stronger connections between their neurons.
be less likely to suffer from brain diseases.
be born with a greater number of neurons.
have better blood flow to their brains.

questions.prompt: Altering the chemistry of the brain with drugs

options.text: is likely to be commonplace in about 40 years.
has had positive outcomes in animals.
is expected to result in greatly improved brain function.
has been shown to have few negative side effects.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the use of ginkgo

options.text: has been supported by a number of neuroscientists.
has had little effect on Alzheimer patients.
has been proved to lessen the impact of disease on the brain.
has been used in medicine for hundreds of years.

subtitle: While it may not be possible to completely age-proof our brains, new anti-aging research shows that our brains may be far more flexible than we thought
